wave-001.question: In Young's double-slit experiment, the slit spacing is 0.5 mm, the distance from the slits to the screen is 1 m, and light with a wavelength of 500 nm is used. Which value is closest to the spacing of the bright fringes on the screen? (Use the approximation L ≫ d.)
choices: About 0.5 mm
About 2.0 mm
About 1.0 mm
wave-001.explanation: Between adjacent bright fringes, the path difference from the two slits changes by exactly one wavelength, so the spacing is Δx = λL/d = 500×10⁻⁹ × 1 / 0.5×10⁻³ = 1.0×10⁻³ m = 1.0 mm. About 0.5 mm divides by 2 as λL/(2d), which is the spacing between a bright and a dark fringe (half a period). About 2.0 mm confuses this with the width of the central maximum of a single slit, 2λL/a. Narrowing the slit spacing or using a longer wavelength spreads the fringes. Besides showing that light is a wave, this experiment is also a way to probe the spatial coherence of a source from how visible the fringes are.

wave-002.question: A source has a center wavelength of 1550 nm and a spectral width of 0.1 nm. Which value is closest to its coherence length (a rough measure of the path difference over which fringes are visible, lc ≈ λ²/Δλ)?
choices: About 24 mm
About 2.4 mm
About 24 µm
wave-002.explanation: The coherence length is lc ≈ λ²/Δλ = (1550×10⁻⁹)² / (0.1×10⁻⁹) ≈ 2.4×10⁻² m, or about 24 mm (the coefficient changes slightly with the spectral shape). About 2.4 mm and about 24 µm are order-of-magnitude errors in converting between nm and m. The narrower the spectrum, the longer the coherence length; a narrow-linewidth laser of around 100 kHz linewidth reaches the kilometer scale. Broadband sources such as white light or an SLD (superluminescent diode), by contrast, have coherence lengths from micrometers to a few tens of micrometers, and OCT (optical coherence tomography) uses this shortness to locate depth.

wave-003.question: A single-layer anti-reflection coating is applied to glass with a refractive index of 1.5, for light at normal incidence from the air side. Which condition makes the reflection zero at the design wavelength?
choices: A coating index of about 1.25 and a physical thickness of a quarter wavelength
A coating index of about 1.22 and an optical thickness of half a wavelength
A coating index of about 1.22 and an optical thickness (index × thickness) of a quarter wavelength
wave-003.explanation: To cancel the two beams reflected from the top and bottom of the coating, the round-trip path difference must be half a wavelength (optical thickness nd = λ/4), and the two reflections must have equal amplitude. The second condition gives a coating index of n = √(n₀ns) = √(1.0 × 1.5) ≈ 1.22. About 1.25 wrongly uses the arithmetic mean (1.0 + 1.5)/2. Making the physical thickness λ/4 overlooks that the wavelength inside the coating shrinks to λ/n. A coating with an optical thickness of λ/2 shifts the round trip by one full wavelength, so the reflections reinforce and the reflectance is the same as with no coating (an absentee layer).

wave-004.question: A single-layer anti-reflection coating of magnesium fluoride (MgF₂, refractive index 1.38) is designed for a wavelength of 550 nm. Which value is closest to the physical thickness for a quarter-wave layer?
choices: About 138 nm
About 100 nm
About 199 nm
wave-004.explanation: A quarter-wave layer requires an optical thickness nd = λ/4, so d = λ/(4n) = 550 / (4 × 1.38) ≈ 99.6 nm, or about 100 nm. About 138 nm is λ/4 = 137.5 nm without dividing by the index, and about 199 nm is λ/(2n), a half-wave layer. Because MgF₂'s index of 1.38 is higher than the ideal √1.5 ≈ 1.22, the reflection does not reach zero; the roughly 4% reflection of a glass (n = 1.5) surface only drops to about 1.4%. To reduce reflection further over a wide wavelength range, multilayer coatings that stack high- and low-index films are used.

wave-005.question: Light at 1550 nm is incident normally from air onto a flat silicon surface with a refractive index of 3.48. Which value is closest to the reflectance at the surface? (Ignore absorption.)
choices: About 4%
About 55%
About 31%
wave-005.explanation: The Fresnel reflectance at normal incidence is R = ((n − 1)/(n + 1))², which for silicon is ((3.48 − 1)/(3.48 + 1))² = (2.48/4.48)² ≈ 0.306, or about 31%. About 4% is the value for glass with an index of 1.5; it is much larger for high-index semiconductors. About 55% is the amplitude reflection coefficient (n − 1)/(n + 1) without squaring. Reflection at the facets of silicon or InP chips not only causes coupling loss (about 1.6 dB per facet) but also sends light back into lasers and creates Fabry–Perot ripples in the transmission of waveguides, so it is suppressed with anti-reflection coatings or angled facets.

wave-006.question: In a Michelson interferometer using a 632.8 nm He-Ne laser, the movable mirror is translated and 1000 bright fringes pass the detector. Which value is closest to the distance the mirror moved? (Take the refractive index of air as 1.)
choices: About 633 µm
About 316 µm
About 158 µm
wave-006.explanation: Moving the mirror by d changes the path difference by 2d, because the light travels to the mirror and back. One fringe passes each time the path difference changes by one wavelength, so 2d = Nλ gives d = 1000 × 632.8 nm / 2 ≈ 316 µm. About 633 µm ignores the round trip and treats the mirror displacement as equal to the path difference; about 158 µm divides by 4 instead. This principle is the basis of laser interferometric length measurement, which uses the wavelength as a ruler. Practical instruments obtain two signals 90° apart with two detectors to tell the direction of motion, and subdivide each fringe further to reach nanometer resolution.

wave-007.question: Which value is closest to the free spectral range (FSR, the frequency spacing between adjacent transmission peaks) of an air-filled Fabry–Perot resonator with a mirror spacing of 10 mm? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 15 GHz
About 30 GHz
About 7.5 GHz
wave-007.explanation: Resonance requires the round-trip optical path 2nL to be an integer number of wavelengths, so adjacent resonance frequencies are spaced by FSR = c/(2nL) = 3.0×10⁸ / (2 × 1 × 0.01) = 1.5×10¹⁰ Hz = 15 GHz. About 30 GHz forgets the round trip and uses c/(nL); about 7.5 GHz is like counting two round trips (4nL). The FSR sets the frequency range that can be measured: light with a wider bandwidth overlaps with the peaks of the next order and can no longer be distinguished. A shorter resonator has a wider FSR, and the same formula sets the longitudinal mode spacing of a laser.

wave-008.question: A Fabry–Perot resonator has a free spectral range (FSR) of 15 GHz and a finesse of 50. Which value is closest to the full width at half maximum of its transmission peaks?
choices: About 750 GHz
About 300 MHz
About 30 MHz
wave-008.explanation: The finesse F is defined as the ratio of the FSR to the full width at half maximum δν of the transmission peaks, F = FSR/δν. So δν = 15 GHz / 50 = 0.3 GHz = 300 MHz. About 750 GHz multiplies instead of dividing; a linewidth wider than the FSR makes no sense. About 30 MHz is an order-of-magnitude error. The higher the mirror reflectance R, the larger the finesse, F ≈ π√R/(1 − R); for example, R = 0.95 gives about 61. High-finesse resonators are used to measure laser linewidths, stabilize frequencies and select wavelengths finely.

wave-009.question: Single-frequency light that satisfies the resonance condition is sent into a Fabry–Perot resonator made of two identical mirrors with no absorption or scattering. If the mirror reflectance is 99%, what is the transmittance?
choices: Nearly 100%
About 1% (1 − R)
wave-009.explanation: The transmittance of a lossless symmetric Fabry–Perot resonator is T = 1 / (1 + F' sin²(δ/2)) (F' = 4R/(1 − R)², δ is the round-trip phase). At resonance, δ = 2πm, the sine term vanishes and T = 1 regardless of the reflectance. The light builds up through many round trips inside the resonator, and the light reflected at the input mirror cancels the light leaking back out of the resonator. The 1% transmittance of one mirror, or the product for two mirrors (1 − R)², assumes the light simply passes through each mirror once and ignores the multiple-beam interference of resonance. Off resonance, the transmittance drops to about (1 − R)²/(1 + R)². In practice, mirror absorption, scattering and imperfect parallelism keep the peak transmittance below 100%.

wave-010.question: Light at 633 nm is incident normally on a transmission grating with 1200 grooves per mm. Which value is closest to the first-order diffraction angle (measured from the grating normal)?
choices: About 41°
About 22°
About 49°
wave-010.explanation: From the grating equation d sinθm = mλ, the grating period is d = 1 mm / 1200 ≈ 833 nm. For the first order (m = 1), sinθ = 633/833 ≈ 0.760, so θ ≈ 49°. About 41° comes from using arccos or measuring the angle from the grating surface; about 22° is the value for a grating with 600 grooves per mm. The second order would need sinθ = 1.52, which exceeds 1, so it does not exist. With more grooves, a grating has greater angular dispersion and separates wavelengths more finely in a spectrometer, but the usable wavelength range and number of orders become narrower.

wave-011.question: A 10 mm diameter collimated beam (wavelength 1.064 µm) is focused by an aberration-free lens with a focal length of 100 mm. Which value is closest to the radius of the first dark ring of the Airy pattern in the focal plane? (Assume a uniformly illuminated circular aperture.)
choices: About 6.5 µm
About 1.3 µm
About 13 µm
wave-011.explanation: The angle of the first dark ring of diffraction from a circular aperture is θ ≈ 1.22λ/D = 1.22 × 1.064×10⁻⁶ / 0.01 ≈ 1.30×10⁻⁴ rad. The radius in the focal plane is r = fθ = 0.1 × 1.30×10⁻⁴ ≈ 1.3×10⁻⁵ m, or about 13 µm. About 6.5 µm treats 1.22λ/D as a full-width angle and halves it; about 1.3 µm is an order-of-magnitude error. About 84% of the total energy falls inside the bright central disk (the Airy disk). Note that a laser beam has a Gaussian rather than uniform profile, so the actual focused spot size is better found with the Gaussian-beam formula (w ≈ λf/(πw₀)).

wave-012.question: In a Michelson interferometer illuminated with white (broadband) light, under what condition can interference fringes be observed?
choices: Fringes are visible only when the path difference between the two arms is nearly zero (within a few micrometers)
Fringes are visible at any path difference, however large, as long as it is an integer multiple of the wavelength, just as with monochromatic light
White light has no fixed phase relationship, so it does not interfere and no fringes are visible at any path difference
wave-012.explanation: Even white light interferes with itself when split from the same source. However, the fringe spacing differs for each wavelength, so as the path difference grows the fringes overlap and wash out; they are visible only within the coherence length, which is shorter for wider bandwidths and only about 1 µm for white light. At zero path difference the fringes of all wavelengths coincide, so just a few colored fringes appear. Fringes at integer multiples of the wavelength apply to monochromatic light, not broadband light. White-light interferometers that measure surface height or film thickness, and OCT, use this property to locate the zero-path-difference point precisely from where the fringes peak.

wave-013.question: In Fraunhofer diffraction from a single slit, how does the central maximum change when the slit width is halved?
choices: The angular width of the central maximum narrows to about half
The angular width of the central maximum roughly doubles
Changing the slit width does not change the angular width
wave-013.explanation: For a slit of width a, the first dark fringe appears at the angle satisfying a sinθ = λ, so the angular width of the central maximum is about 2λ/a. Halving the width roughly doubles the angular width. The rule that a smaller aperture spreads light more by diffraction is the same as for beam divergence (λ/(πw₀)) and the Airy disk (1.22λ/D). Narrowing to half reverses the relation between aperture and spread, and no change is the geometric-shadow way of thinking. A narrower slit both spreads the light and passes less of it, so the central intensity drops sharply.

wave-014.question: Why are many layers of films with different refractive indices stacked in dielectric multilayer mirrors and bandpass filters?
choices: Because stacking thicker films absorbs more light, which raises the reflectance just as in a metal mirror
Because the reflections from each boundary interfere to reinforce (or cancel), giving high reflectance or sharp wavelength characteristics
Because with more layers, errors in each layer average out and the characteristics become independent of angle of incidence and polarization
wave-014.explanation: Alternating high- and low-index films, each with an optical thickness of λ/4, makes the light reflected at every boundary add in phase, and adding layers raises the reflectance to 99.9% or more. This periodic structure is a Bragg mirror with a reflection band, also used as the mirrors of VCSEL semiconductor lasers. Changing the design gives narrow-passband filters or broadband anti-reflection coatings. Unlike metal mirrors, dielectric coatings work with almost no absorption. Because multilayer characteristics are set by interference, they depend on angle of incidence and polarization; tilting the filter shifts its passband toward shorter wavelengths.

wave-015.question: Two coherent beams (with the same polarization) with an intensity ratio of 1:4 are overlapped to interfere. Which value is closest to the fringe visibility (Imax − Imin)/(Imax + Imin)?
wave-015.explanation: For two-beam interference, I = I₁ + I₂ + 2√(I₁I₂) cosδ, so the visibility is V = 2√(I₁I₂)/(I₁ + I₂). With I₁ = 1 and I₂ = 4, V = 2 × 2 / 5 = 0.8. 0.6 wrongly uses the intensity difference (4 − 1)/(4 + 1), and 1.0 is obtained only when the intensities are equal. Even with a fourfold intensity mismatch, the amplitude ratio is only 2, so the visibility does not drop much. In practice, mismatched polarization and insufficient source coherence also reduce visibility, so matching the power and polarization in both arms is basic practice in interferometers.

wave-016.question: When a vertical soap film is lit with white light and viewed in reflection, the top part, where the liquid has drained and the film has become very thin, looks black with no color. Which correctly explains the reflection there?
choices: Only one of the two surface reflections is phase-shifted by π, so when the film is much thinner than the wavelength the reflections cancel
Both surface reflections have a phase shift of π, so a thin film makes the two reflected waves add up, giving every color the same brightness
The thinner the film, the larger the fraction of light absorbed by the liquid, so all wavelengths are absorbed and no light is reflected
wave-016.explanation: Reflection at the front surface, going from low-index air toward the liquid, shifts the phase by π, while reflection at the back surface, going from the liquid toward air, does not. This π is added to the round-trip path difference 2nd, so when the thickness d is much smaller than the wavelength the two reflections are out of phase and cancel, weakening the reflection at every wavelength and making the film look black. If both reflections were shifted by π, a thin film would instead reinforce and look bright, which disagrees with observation. A thinner film has less liquid for light to pass through, so the absorption explanation is backward. The colors of thicker regions arise because the condition for reinforcement differs with wavelength.

wave-017.question: Two flat glass plates 100 mm long are stacked with a thin wire 20 µm in diameter inserted at one end, forming a wedge-shaped air layer. When light of wavelength 600 nm illuminates it from directly above, which value is closest to the spacing of the interference fringes seen in reflection? Take the refractive index of air as 1.
choices: About 3.0 mm
About 1.0 mm
About 1.5 mm
wave-017.explanation: The wedge angle is θ = 20 µm / 100 mm = 2×10⁻⁴ rad. Where the air layer is t thick, the round-trip path difference is 2t, so adjacent dark fringes differ in thickness by λ/2 and the fringe spacing is λ/(2θ) = 600×10⁻⁹ / (2 × 2×10⁻⁴) = 1.5 mm. About 3.0 mm ignores the round trip and takes the thickness step as λ, and about 1.0 mm divides by the glass index 1.5 even though the layer is air. The fringes are contours of equal air thickness, so they can be used to check the flatness of plates, and the wire diameter can be worked out from the fringe spacing.

wave-018.question: A double slit with spacing d is replaced by a grating with many slits at the same spacing d, illuminated by the same monochromatic light. Which correctly describes how the bright fringes seen far away change?
choices: The more slits there are, the smaller the angular spacing between fringes, which crowd together in inverse proportion to the number of slits
The angles of the bright fringes (d sinθ = mλ) stay the same, and the more slits there are, the narrower and sharper each fringe becomes
Neither the angles nor the widths change; with more slits, each bright fringe just becomes brighter in proportion to the number of slits
wave-018.explanation: The directions of the bright fringes (principal maxima) are set by the condition that the path difference d sinθ between neighboring slits is an integer number of wavelengths, so they appear at the same angles as for a double slit regardless of the number of slits N. Only in these directions are all N waves in phase; a slight change of angle spreads their phases and they cancel, so each principal maximum narrows to about 1/N, with N − 2 weak secondary maxima in between. The amplitude of a principal maximum is N times larger, so its intensity grows as N², not merely in proportion to N. The fringe spacing is fixed by the slit spacing d and does not depend on the number of slits. This sharpness is what lets a grating separate wavelengths finely.

wave-019.question: When a laser beam shines on a thin hair, a diffraction pattern much like that of a single slit appears on a screen, and the hair's thickness can be found from the fringe spacing. Which principle justifies this method?
choices: Babinet's principle: complementary obstacles and apertures (the hair and a slit of the same width) give the same diffraction pattern except at the center reached by the direct light
Thin-film interference between light reflected from the front and back of the hair, with the fringe spacing set by the product of the hair's index and thickness
Double-slit interference between two beams passing either side of the hair, with the fringe spacing set by the beam diameter rather than the hair's thickness
wave-019.explanation: Babinet's principle states that the field passing through an aperture plus the field passing around the complementary obstacle equals the field with nothing in the way. An unobstructed collimated beam reaches only the central point in the far field, so everywhere else the two diffracted fields are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign, and their intensity patterns are identical. A hair of thickness a therefore produces the same fringes as a single slit of width a, and its thickness follows from the dark-fringe angles sinθ = mλ/a. The fringes are not thin-film interference from surface reflections, and their spacing is set by the width of the obstacle, not the beam diameter.

wave-020.question: Light from a distant star produces double-slit interference fringes, but light from a large extended source placed close by (such as a bulb behind frosted glass) produces almost none. Which property explains the difference?
choices: Starlight has a narrow, nearly monochromatic spectrum, so its temporal coherence is high, and fringe visibility depends only on spectral width
The smaller the angle a source subtends, the more the light at two separated points stays in step (the higher its spatial coherence)
Starlight is amplified by stimulated emission over its long path through space, so it arrives with its phases aligned like laser light
wave-020.explanation: For the light at two slits to form fringes, the phase relation between the two points must not wander over time; this is spatial coherence. Each point of an extended source radiates independently, so if the source subtends an angle θs, the phases stay correlated only for slit separations smaller than roughly λ/θs (the van Cittert–Zernike theorem). A star subtends an extremely small angle, so its light stays spatially coherent over large separations. Starlight is also broadband and nearly white, so spectral width cannot explain the difference, and it is not amplified into phase-aligned light along the way. Michelson's stellar interferometer measured stars' angular diameters from the separation at which the fringes vanished.

wave-021.question: The convex face of a plano-convex lens with a radius of curvature of 2.0 m rests on a flat glass plate, and light with a wavelength of 589 nm illuminates it from directly above; Newton's rings are observed in reflection. Counting the central dark spot as number 0, which value is closest to the radius of the 10th dark ring? (Take the air-gap thickness at radius r to be t ≈ r²/(2R).)
choices: About 4.9 mm
About 2.4 mm
About 3.4 mm
wave-021.explanation: Only the reflection at the lower surface of the air gap (the glass plate) has a phase shift of π, so the reflected light is dark when the round-trip path difference 2t equals an integer number of wavelengths, mλ. Substituting t ≈ r²/(2R) gives r² = mλR, so r = √(10 × 589×10⁻⁹ × 2.0) ≈ 3.4×10⁻³ m, about 3.4 mm. About 4.9 mm ignores the round trip and sets t = mλ, and about 2.4 mm overestimates the gap thickness by a factor of two, as r²/R. The ring radius is proportional to √m, so the outer rings are more closely spaced. Measuring the ring radii gives the radius of curvature of the lens or the wavelength of the light.

wave-022.question: When laser light illuminates a rough surface such as paper or paint, the lit area looks like a fine pattern of bright and dark spots (speckle). Which correctly explains the cause of this pattern?
choices: Many coherent scattered waves, with phases randomized by the surface roughness, interfere and reinforce or cancel from place to place
The surface roughness diffracts each wavelength in a different direction, so slight wavelength differences within the laser light separate and appear as color mottling
Each bump on the surface focuses light like a lens, and the foci line up as bright points, so the shape of the roughness is imaged directly
wave-022.explanation: Laser light is coherent both spatially and temporally, so light scattered from each point of a surface whose roughness is comparable to or larger than the wavelength overlaps with fixed phase relationships. Because the roughness randomizes the phases, the waves reinforce or cancel differently at each observation point, producing a random pattern of bright and dark spots. The pattern changes when the eye moves because it is the result of interference, not an image of the roughness. Speckle appears even with nearly monochromatic laser light, so it is not color separation due to wavelength differences. With the low-coherence light of an incandescent lamp the spots average out and disappear. Speckle degrades the image quality of laser projection, but it is also used to measure surface displacement and strain.

wave-023.question: When monochromatic light from a point source illuminates a small opaque disk, a bright spot (the Poisson spot, or Arago spot) appears exactly at the center of the disk's shadow. Which correctly explains why this bright spot forms?
choices: Light reflected from the side face at the disk's edge heads into the shadow as if from a mirror and converges to a single point on the central axis
The diffracted light bending around each point of the disk edge reaches the central axis with the same optical path length and adds up in phase
Light that passes faintly through the disk is refracted within its thickness and gathered toward the shadow's center as by a lens
wave-023.explanation: By the Huygens–Fresnel principle, each point on the circle around the edge of the disk acts as a new source. Every point on this circle is the same distance from a point on the disk's central axis, so all the light diffracted around the edge arrives in phase and adds up, producing a bright spot at the center of the shadow. In the 19th century Poisson pointed this out as an absurd consequence of Fresnel's wave theory, and Arago's experimental confirmation helped the wave theory of light gain wide acceptance. An opaque disk transmits no light, and reflection from its edge is not directed toward the central axis, so neither reflection nor refraction can explain the spot. If the edge is not a smooth circle, the spot becomes blurred.

wave-024.question: A diffraction-grating spectrometer uses first-order diffraction to measure the range 600–900 nm. If the source also contains light at 400 nm, its second-order diffraction emerges at the same angle as the first order of some other wavelength and disturbs the measurement. Which correctly gives the overlapping first-order wavelength and the remedy?
choices: It emerges at the same angle as first-order 200 nm, so the 600–900 nm measurement range is not affected
It emerges at the same angle as first-order 800 nm, so a grating with more grooves should be used to raise the resolving power and separate them
It emerges at the same angle as first-order 800 nm, so a filter that blocks short wavelengths (an order-sorting filter) should be inserted
wave-024.explanation: In the grating equation d sinθ = mλ, the angle is set by the product mλ of the order and the wavelength. For 400 nm in second order, mλ = 800 nm, so it emerges at the same angle as 800 nm in first order and cannot be distinguished on the detector. Taking 200 nm divides by the order where it should be multiplied. Increasing the number of grooves to raise the resolving power mN cannot separate light that overlaps at the same angle. The standard remedy is to insert a long-pass colored-glass filter that blocks wavelengths shorter than the measurement range beforehand. The range that can be measured in first order alone without overlap runs from the shortest wavelength to twice that wavelength; this is called the free spectral range of the grating.

wave-025.question: The hypotenuse faces of two right-angle prisms are placed facing each other with a very narrow air gap, about a wavelength wide, and light is launched at an angle that produces total internal reflection at the face of one prism. Which correctly describes what happens?
choices: Because the condition for total internal reflection is met, all the light is reflected however narrow the gap, and none enters the other prism
The evanescent wave extending beyond the boundary reaches the other prism, and the narrower the gap, the more light is transmitted
Light undergoes multiple reflections and interferes in the air gap, so half is transmitted and half is reflected regardless of the gap width
wave-025.explanation: Even under total internal reflection, an evanescent wave extends beyond the boundary, decaying exponentially with distance from it (the penetration depth is about a wavelength). When the second prism is brought within about a wavelength, this field becomes a propagating wave again and is transmitted into the other side, and the reflection drops accordingly. This is called frustrated total internal reflection, and it has the same form as quantum-mechanical tunneling. The transmittance varies exponentially with the gap width, so it is not fixed at one half, and widening the gap returns the reflection to nearly 100%. The fact that the field outside the boundary is not zero even under total internal reflection is also the principle behind directional couplers and prism couplers.

wave-026.question: Collimated light with a wavelength of 800 nm illuminates a circular aperture 2 mm in diameter. When the distance z from the aperture is much larger than D²/λ (D is the aperture diameter), the pattern can be treated as far-field (Fraunhofer) diffraction. Which value is closest to this guide distance D²/λ?
choices: About 5 mm
About 5 m
About 1.3 m
wave-026.explanation: D²/λ = (2×10⁻³ m)² / (800×10⁻⁹ m) = 5 m. Well beyond this distance from the aperture, the phase differences between light from different points of the aperture depend only on the viewing angle, and the pattern becomes Fraunhofer diffraction, which grows in proportion to distance without changing shape. Closer in, in the Fresnel region, the shape of the pattern itself changes with distance. About 5 mm comes from a mistake converting mm and m. About 1.3 m puts the radius (1 mm) instead of the diameter into the D²/λ defined here. Some books use a²/λ with the radius a as the guide, so the factor depends on convention; check which length the formula uses. In the focal plane of a lens the Fraunhofer pattern appears even at short distances.

wave-027.question: In Young's double-slit experiment with monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm, just one slit is covered by a thin transparent film 6.0 µm thick with a refractive index of 1.5. Which correctly describes the change in the fringes on the screen?
choices: The fringe spacing is unchanged and the pattern shifts by 5 fringes toward the covered slit
The fringe spacing is unchanged and the pattern shifts by 5 fringes away from the covered slit
The fringe spacing is unchanged and the pattern shifts by 15 fringes toward the covered slit
wave-027.explanation: The optical path through the film is longer than through air alone by (n − 1)t = 0.5 × 6.0 µm = 3.0 µm. That is 3.0 µm / 0.6 µm = 5 wavelengths, so the pattern shifts by 5 fringes. The central bright fringe, where the optical path difference is zero, moves to where the geometric path from the covered slit is shorter, that is, toward the covered slit. The fringe spacing λL/d does not depend on the film and stays the same. 15 fringes comes from using nt/λ without subtracting the air path. A shift away from the covered slit takes the wrong direction for compensating the extra optical path. The fringe shift can be used to measure the thickness or index of a thin film.

wave-028.question: In the X-ray region, the refractive index of most materials is slightly less than 1 (about 1 − 10⁻⁶), so the phase velocity c/n in the material exceeds the speed of light in vacuum c. Which statement about this is correct?
choices: Because the phase velocity exceeds c, X-rays can carry information and energy through matter faster than light
A refractive index below 1 would violate relativity, so it must be a measurement error, and the true index is always at least 1 at every wavelength
Information and energy are carried at the group velocity of a wave packet, so a phase velocity above c does not violate relativity
wave-028.explanation: The phase velocity is the speed at which the crests of a wave of constant amplitude move, and by itself it carries no signal. Information and energy travel with changes in amplitude (wave packets), at the group velocity, and in the X-ray region the group velocity stays below c even though the index is below 1. Far above the resonances, electrons oscillate out of phase with the field, so the polarization points opposite to the field and n < 1. An index below 1 is a measured property: X-rays striking a surface at a grazing angle undergo total reflection from the vacuum side into the material (total external reflection), which is used in grazing-incidence X-ray mirrors.

wave-029.question: Two independent lasers emit light of the same intensity I and the same polarization (slightly different frequencies, with no fixed phase relation) and illuminate the same spot on a screen. Which correctly gives the intensity averaged over a time much longer than the detector response time?
choices: At every point the square of the summed amplitudes gives constructive interference and a uniform intensity of 4I
The phase difference changes with time and the interference term averages to zero, giving 2I
Light without a fixed phase relation cancels more often than it adds, so the average is darker than I
wave-029.explanation: The combined intensity is I₁ + I₂ + 2√(I₁I₂) cosΔφ. For independent lasers the phase difference Δφ changes with time, so over a long average the cosΔφ term vanishes and the intensity is the simple sum I + I = 2I. 4I occurs only at points where coherent light overlaps in phase, and even then the dark parts of the fringes are zero, so the overall average is 2I and energy is conserved. Light without a fixed phase relation does not cancel more often than it reinforces, so the average never drops below I.

wave-030.question: Two coherent beams split from the same source (with a path difference much shorter than the coherence length) are overlapped. One is horizontally linearly polarized and the other vertically. Which statement about their interference is correct?
choices: The fields are orthogonal, so the interference term vanishes; the intensity stays the sum of the two and no fringes appear as the path difference changes
Because the light is coherent it interferes whatever the polarization, and fringes appear as the path difference changes
Orthogonal polarizations cancel each other, so the intensity where the beams overlap is zero whatever the path difference
wave-030.explanation: The interference term is proportional to the dot product E₁·E₂ of the two fields, so it is zero for orthogonal linear polarizations and the intensity remains I₁ + I₂ (the Fresnel–Arago laws). Changing the path difference only changes the polarization of the combined light through linear, elliptical and circular states; no intensity fringes form. Saying they interfere regardless of polarization assumes coherence alone decides interference. Nor does the intensity drop to zero; energy is conserved. Placing a polarizer at 45° to both polarizations after the beams selects a common component, and fringes appear. This is why the polarizations of the two beams must be matched in an interferometer.

wave-031.question: A single-layer antireflection coating of magnesium fluoride (MgF₂, refractive index 1.38) with an optical thickness of λ/4 is applied to glass with a refractive index of 1.52. Which value is closest to the reflectance at the design wavelength at normal incidence? (Take the index of air as 1.0, ignore absorption, and use R = ((n₀nₛ − n₁²)/(n₀nₛ + n₁²))².)
choices: 0% (fully cancelled)
About 1.3%
About 4.3%
wave-031.explanation: In a λ/4 layer the reflections from the top and bottom of the film are half a wavelength apart and cancel, but the reflection vanishes only when the two reflected amplitudes are equal. That requires n₁ = √(n₀nₛ) ≈ 1.23; MgF₂ at 1.38 is higher, so the cancellation is incomplete. R = ((1.52 − 1.38²)/(1.52 + 1.38²))² = ((1.52 − 1.904)/(1.52 + 1.904))² ≈ 0.0126, so about 1.3% remains. 0% assumes that the λ/4 thickness alone removes the reflection. About 4.3% is the reflectance of the uncoated glass surface, ((1.52 − 1)/(1.52 + 1))², which ignores the coating. Multilayer coatings are used to reduce the reflection further.

wave-032.question: Light with a wavelength of 633 nm is incident normally on a transmission grating with 600 grooves per mm. Which range of diffraction orders appears? (Use the grating equation d sinθ = mλ.)
choices: Up to ±1st order (3 beams including the 0th order)
Up to ±3rd order (7 beams including the 0th order)
Up to ±2nd order (5 beams including the 0th order)
wave-032.explanation: The groove spacing is d = 1/600 mm ≈ 1.667 µm. The diffraction angle follows sinθ = mλ/d, and since sinθ cannot exceed 1, |m| ≤ d/λ = 1.667/0.633 ≈ 2.63, so five beams appear: m = 0, ±1 and ±2. The first order leaves at about 22.3° and the second at about 49.4°. Up to ±3rd order rounds d/λ up; for the third order sinθ ≈ 1.14, so no propagating diffracted beam exists. Up to ±1st order applies when d/λ is smaller than 2, as for a grating with 1200 grooves/mm. The finer the grooves, the fewer orders appear, and gratings for spectrometers are designed to concentrate light into the order that is used.

wave-033.question: Monochromatic light from a point source and the same light reflected from a plane mirror at grazing incidence overlap on a screen and form interference fringes (Lloyd's mirror). Which fringe appears where the plane of the mirror, extended, meets the screen (the point where the two optical paths are equal)?
choices: A dark fringe, because reflection shifts the phase by π, so the waves cancel even though the paths are equal
A bright fringe, because the two paths are equal, just like the central fringe of Young's experiment
Uniform brightness without fringes, because only an evanescent wave reaches the mirror surface
wave-033.explanation: In Lloyd's mirror the image of the source in the mirror acts as a second source, producing fringes of the same form as Young's double slit. Light reflected from the mirror at grazing incidence, however, undergoes a phase shift of π (half a wavelength). On the extension of the mirror plane the two optical paths are equal, so only this π shift remains, and the waves cancel to give a dark fringe. Expecting a bright fringe because the paths are equal forgets the phase change on reflection; the whole fringe pattern is shifted by half a period compared with a double slit. An evanescent wave is the field that leaks beyond the boundary in total internal reflection and plays no role here. This dark fringe is known as a direct demonstration that reflection changes the phase by π.

wave-034.question: Interferometers are classified as wavefront-division or amplitude-division types according to how they split one beam into two. Which combination of classification and property is correct for Young's double slit and the Michelson interferometer?
choices: Both divide the wavefront, so fringes have the same contrast with an extended source as with a point source
The double slit divides the amplitude and the Michelson divides the wavefront, so the Michelson shows fringes only with a point source
The double slit divides the wavefront and needs a small source; the Michelson divides the amplitude and shows fringes even with an extended source
wave-034.explanation: The double slit takes light from two different places on the wavefront (the two slits), so it is a wavefront-division interferometer. Light from two points interferes only if their phases are correlated, and a large source lowers the spatial coherence and washes out the fringes, so the source is made small with a pinhole or similar. The Michelson interferometer splits the amplitude of the same beam with a beam splitter; light from each point of the source interferes with itself, so fringes are visible even with an extended source (the fringes are localized, for example at infinity). The reversed classification and the claim that both divide the wavefront are wrong. Thin-film interference and the Fabry–Perot resonator are also amplitude-division interference.

wave-035.question: When the two mirrors of a Michelson interferometer are set exactly perpendicular (so that one mirror and the image of the other are parallel) and the instrument is illuminated with an extended monochromatic source, concentric circular fringes (fringes of equal inclination) are seen. How do the fringes change as the movable mirror is moved to reduce the path difference between the two arms?
choices: New rings keep emerging from the center, and the ring spacing gradually narrows into fine fringes
The rings shrink into the center and vanish, the ring spacing widens, and at zero path difference the field becomes uniform
The concentric rings gradually turn into parallel straight fringes, whose spacing is narrowest at zero path difference
wave-035.explanation: If d is the separation between one mirror and the image of the other, light travelling at an inclination θ has a path difference of 2d cosθ, and bright rings lie at angles satisfying 2d cosθ = mλ. The order is highest at the center (θ = 0); as d decreases, each ring moves toward larger cosθ, that is, toward the center, and the rings disappear there one by one. At the same time the angular separation between neighbouring rings grows, so the ring spacing widens, and at d = 0 the whole field has the same brightness. Rings emerging and becoming finer is what happens when the path difference is increased. Parallel straight fringes are fringes of equal thickness, seen when a mirror is slightly tilted; they do not appear simply by reducing the path difference.

wave-036.question: Monochromatic light enters a Mach–Zehnder interferometer built from two lossless 50:50 beam splitters, and the optical path length of one arm is changed gradually. How do the intensities at the interferometer's two outputs behave?
choices: When one output brightens the other dims, and the sum of the two outputs always equals the input intensity
Both outputs brighten and dim together, and in the dark state the light is turned into heat in the beam splitter
Interference appears at only one output; the other always receives half of the input, whatever the phase difference
wave-036.explanation: If the beam splitters are lossless, energy conservation requires the two outputs to add up to the input intensity. Because of the phase relations between reflection and transmission, constructive interference at one exit is accompanied by destructive interference at the other, and the intensities vary complementarily as cos²(Δφ/2) and sin²(Δφ/2). If both outputs went dark at once, the light would have nowhere to go, which cannot happen in a lossless device. Interference at only one exit is also wrong: both exits show fringes of the same depth in opposite phase. This complementarity is why balanced detection, which takes the difference of the two outputs, doubles the interference signal.

wave-037.question: Collimated monochromatic light illuminates a double slit made of two slits 0.10 mm wide whose centres are 0.30 mm apart. In the far-field pattern, how many interference fringes appear within the central maximum of the single-slit diffraction (inside the first dark lines on either side)?
wave-037.explanation: Interference maxima appear where d sinθ = mλ, and the single-slit diffraction minima where a sinθ = λ. Since d/a = 0.30/0.10 = 3, the third-order interference maximum falls exactly on the first single-slit minimum and vanishes (a missing order). The orders that remain inside the central maximum are m = 0, ±1 and ±2, five fringes in all. Seven also counts the ±3 orders, but the diffracted intensity there is zero, so no fringe is seen. Three takes the ratio d/a directly as the number of fringes; the fringes lie symmetrically on both sides of the zero order, so two on each side plus the zero order must be counted. For the same reason, the ±6 and ±9 orders are also missing.

wave-038.question: White light falls at normal incidence on an oxide film (take its refractive index as 1.46) on a silicon substrate, and the reflectance is measured as a function of wavelength. Adjacent reflectance peaks appear at 600 nm and 500 nm. Which value is closest to the film thickness? (Neglect the wavelength dependence of the refractive index.)
choices: About 1.03 µm
About 1.5 µm
About 2.05 µm
wave-038.explanation: At both the air–film and film–silicon interfaces the light reflects toward a higher index, so the phase shifts cancel and the condition for constructive reflection at normal incidence is 2nt = mλ. Adjacent peaks differ in order m by one, so 2nt/500 − 2nt/600 = 1, giving t = λ₁λ₂/(2n(λ₁ − λ₂)) = 600 × 500/(2 × 1.46 × 100) ≈ 1027 nm, or about 1.03 µm. Then 2nt = 3000 nm, so 600 nm is the fifth-order peak and 500 nm the sixth. About 1.5 µm omits the refractive index, and about 2.05 µm drops the factor of 2 for the round trip.

wave-039.question: When monochromatic light strikes a flat metal mirror at normal incidence, the incident and reflected waves overlap and form a standing wave in front of the mirror. Which combination correctly describes the electric field at the mirror surface and the spacing of the electric-field nodes (planes of zero intensity)? (Treat the mirror as a perfect conductor.)
choices: The surface is an antinode of the electric field, and the nodes repeat every λ/2 starting λ/4 from the mirror
The surface is a node of the electric field, and successive nodes are spaced λ/4 apart
The surface is a node of the electric field, and the nodes repeat every λ/2 from the mirror
wave-039.explanation: At the surface of a perfect conductor the tangential electric field must vanish, so the reflected field is in antiphase with the incident field there and the surface is a node of the electric field. The standing-wave intensity varies as sin²(kz), so the nodes lie at kz = mπ, every λ/2 from the mirror, with antinodes midway at λ/4, 3λ/4 and so on. Taking the surface as an antinode forgets the phase reversal on reflection; it is the magnetic field that has an antinode at the surface. A node spacing of λ/4 confuses the distance between a node and the adjacent antinode with the node spacing. In Wiener's experiment, a thin photographic film laid at a slant over a mirror was exposed at the antinodes of the electric field, showing that it is the electric field that causes exposure.

wave-040.question: A Michelson interferometer used to observe white-light fringes has, besides a plate beam splitter with a partially reflecting coating on one face, a compensator plate of the same glass and thickness placed in one arm, parallel to the beam splitter. What is the role of the compensator plate?
choices: The reflected and transmitted arms carry different intensities, so absorption in the compensator balances the two arms and raises the fringe visibility (the contrast between bright and dark)
Light in one arm crosses the beam-splitter glass two extra times, so the compensator adds the same glass to the other arm and equalizes the path difference at all wavelengths
Passing through the beam-splitter glass rotates the polarization, so the compensator rotates it back and makes the two arms' polarizations match
wave-040.explanation: With a plate coated on one face, light in one arm crosses the glass three times in total and light in the other arm only once, a difference of two plate thicknesses. For monochromatic light this could be offset by moving a mirror, but glass is dispersive, so the required offset differs from wavelength to wavelength, and the white-light fringes, which appear only near zero path difference, wash out. A compensator of the same glass equalizes the glass thickness in both arms, so the path difference goes to zero at all wavelengths at once. The compensator is a clear, non-absorbing plate; it does not balance intensities, and transmission near normal incidence does not rotate the polarization either.

wave-041.question: Let r and t be the amplitude reflection and transmission coefficients for light incident from one side of an interface, and r′ and t′ those for light incident from the other side. Which relation follows from the idea that the ray paths must also hold when traced backward (the Stokes relations)? (Assume no absorption.)
choices: r′ = r and tt′ = 1 − r²
r′ = −r and t = t′ = √(1 − r²)
r′ = −r and tt′ = 1 − r²
wave-041.explanation: If the reflected and transmitted waves are sent back in reverse, only the original incident wave should return, and the light leaving toward the other side must cancel. This condition gives r² + tt′ = 1 and r′ = −r. For normal incidence between air and glass of index 1.5, r = −0.2, r′ = +0.2, t = 0.8 and t′ = 1.2, and indeed tt′ = 0.96 = 1 − r². Taking r′ = r is wrong because it does not produce the phase difference of π between reflections from the two sides. This π difference is why the reflections from a film much thinner than the wavelength cancel. Taking t = t′ is also wrong: the amplitude transmission coefficients differ between the two sides, and it is their product tt′ that is fixed.

wave-042.question: The Fraunhofer diffraction intensity of a single slit of width a is I = I₀ (sinβ/β)² with β = πa sinθ/λ, and the first secondary maximum just outside the central peak lies at β ≈ 1.43π. Approximately what percentage of the central intensity I₀ is the intensity of this secondary maximum?
choices: About 4.7%
About 22%
About 1.7%
wave-042.explanation: At β = 1.43π ≈ 4.49, sinβ ≈ −0.976, so sinβ/β ≈ −0.217, and the intensity, its square, is about 0.047, or about 4.7% of the center. The secondary maxima are solutions of tanβ = β and lie slightly inside the midpoint 1.5π between π and 2π. About 22% takes the amplitude ratio |sinβ/β| directly as the intensity, forgetting to square it. About 1.7% is the value for the first bright ring of the Airy pattern of a circular aperture; for a circular aperture the surrounding rings are even weaker than for a slit. Secondary maxima get weaker farther out, and the second is about 1.6%. This gives a guide to the light around the image of a spectrometer slit or around a beam whose edges are clipped.

wave-043.question: A Fresnel biprism (refractive index 1.5), made of two thin prisms with apex angle α = 1.0° joined at their bases, is placed 0.20 m from a point source (wavelength 589 nm), and the interference fringes are observed on a screen 1.0 m from the source. Taking the separation of the two virtual sources as d = 2a(n − 1)α (a is the source-to-biprism distance and α is in radians), which is closest to the fringe spacing?
choices: About 0.34 mm
About 0.17 mm
About 0.084 mm
wave-043.explanation: The upper and lower halves of the biprism each bend the light by (n − 1)α in opposite directions, creating two virtual sources at the position of the source, separated by d = 2 × 0.20 × 0.5 × 0.01745 ≈ 3.49 mm. The fringe spacing has the same form as for a double slit, Δx = λL/d = 589×10⁻⁹ × 1.0/(3.49×10⁻³) ≈ 1.7×10⁻⁴ m, or about 0.17 mm. About 0.34 mm results from forgetting the factor of 2 for the two halves bending in opposite directions, which halves d. About 0.084 mm results from forgetting to multiply by (n − 1) and taking the bending angle as α itself. The biprism is a wavefront-division interferometer that overlaps two beams split from one source without using slits.

wave-044.question: A narrow laser beam strikes a glass-to-air interface at an angle of incidence larger than the critical angle and is totally reflected. Which correctly describes the Goos–Hänchen effect seen when the reflected beam is examined precisely?
choices: The reflection angle deviates slightly from the law of reflection, becoming larger than the angle of incidence, so the beam leaves in a direction tilted away from the interface
Part of the light leaks away through the evanescent wave that penetrates beyond the interface, so even total internal reflection loses a few percent of reflectance
The reflected beam emerges from a position shifted sideways along the interface by roughly a wavelength, and the size of the shift differs between polarizations
wave-044.explanation: In total internal reflection an evanescent wave penetrates beyond the interface, and the phase of the reflection depends on the angle of incidence. A narrow beam is a collection of plane waves at slightly different angles, and the different phases of these components add up to shift the reflected beam sideways along the interface. This is the Goos–Hänchen effect; the shift is small, of the order of a wavelength, and differs between s- and p-polarization. The reflection angle itself obeys the law of reflection and does not become larger. Total internal reflection in a lossless medium has a reflectance of 100%, and the evanescent wave carries no energy away unless another medium is brought close on the far side. In waveguide mode calculations this shift increases the effective thickness of the guide.

wave-045.question: Windows and substrates placed in a laser beam path are often polished not with their two faces exactly parallel but with a slight angle (a wedge). What is the main reason?
choices: Overlapping reflections from the two faces form a weak Fabry–Perot resonator whose transmission ripples with wavelength and temperature, and tilting the reflections apart prevents this
The prism action of the wedge separates the directions of different wavelengths, so unwanted wavelengths mixed into the laser light can be removed behind the window
Parallel faces rotate the polarization of the transmitted light, so tilting the faces cancels the effect of birefringence in the window material and preserves polarization
wave-045.explanation: Two parallel faces act as a low-finesse Fabry–Perot resonator even when their reflectance is only a few percent. For a window with index 1.45 and thickness 5 mm the FSR is about 21 GHz, and a reflectance of about 3.4% on each face makes the transmission ripple periodically over a range of about 13%, so tiny changes in wavelength, temperature or tilt change the output or produce interference fringes. With a wedge, the reflections from the two faces leave in different directions and do not overlap, and the ripple disappears. The wedge angle is small and bends the light only slightly, with nowhere near enough dispersion to separate wavelengths. Parallel faces do not rotate the polarization, and the wedge is not a measure against birefringence.
